evidence: src/presentation/http/LoanController.ts: `lend(body: LendRequest): Promise<HttpResult>` returns `{ status: 201, body: renderLoan(loan) }`. Building the HTTP response is presentation work.
src/presentation/http/LoanController.ts: the constructor injects LendingService and LoanHistoryService from src/business/services (domain layer, an allowed dependency). This is dependency wiring.
src/presentation/http/LoanController.ts: `giveBack` takes the fine from `this.lending.giveBack(body.loanId, new Date())`. The fine is calculated in the business layer, not in the controller.
src/presentation/http/LoanController.ts: `this.history.note(loan.id, 'lent')` is a plain call to a business service with no rule or branching around it.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: LoanController sits in the presentation layer, and everything it declares fits that role. LendRequest and ReturnRequest are request DTOs. The handlers return the project's own HttpResult type with status codes 201 and 200 and render the body through renderLoan from the presentation views. The constructor injects LendingService and LoanHistoryService from the business layer, which presentation is allowed to depend on, so that is dependency wiring. The file computes no fines, does no validation and makes no domain decisions. The fine comes back from lending.giveBack, and the loan comes from lending.lend. Calling history.note after each operation is a sequence of calls into business services that are allowed dependencies, with no logic or branching of its own, so I treat it as orchestration rather than a misplaced business rule. This is the only borderline point. One could argue that "every lend is recorded" is a business invariant that should live in the business layer, but there is no calculation or decision in the controller itself. The file does no direct I/O and has no framework decorators or base classes. No candidate flags were raised.
